items.title: Eight Recurring Necessities of Daily Life

items.zh: 云何八數隨行？謂諸世間數數隨所行事。一、蔽覆事，二、瑩飾身事，三、威儀易奪事，四、飲食事，五、睡眠事，六、交會事，七、屬彼勤劬事，八、屬彼言說事。
items.en: What are the eight recurring necessities? They are the things worldly beings must attend to again and again. First, the matter of covering the body. Second, the matter of adorning and cleansing the body. Third, the matter of shifting one's posture. Fourth, the matter of eating and drinking. Fifth, the matter of sleep. Sixth, the matter of social gathering. Seventh, the matter of bodily labour. Eighth, the matter of speech.

items.title: Three Worldly Affairs, and Three Kinds of Speech

items.zh: 云何三種世事？一、語言談論，更相慶慰事；二、嫁娶賓主，更相飲噉事；三、於起作種種事中，更相營助事。
items.en: What are the three worldly affairs? First, conversing together in mutual celebration and comfort. Second, weddings and the hosting of guests, eating and drinking together. Third, helping one another in the various undertakings of life.

items.zh: 云何三種語言？謂有法語言、無法語言，及餘語言。有法語言者，謂宣說厭捨，離諸纏蓋趣可愛樂等。廣說如經。無法語言者，謂染污心說飲食等。餘語言者，謂無記心所起言說。
items.en: What are the three kinds of speech? Speech in accord with the Dharma; speech not in accord with the Dharma; and all other speech. Speech in accord with the Dharma is that which teaches renunciation, freedom from the various entanglements and hindrances, and the attainment of what is truly to be delighted in — as explained at length in the sūtras. Speech not in accord with the Dharma is speech about food, drink, and the like, spoken with a defiled mind. All other speech is that which arises from a mind that is neither wholesome nor unwholesome.

items.zh: 云何二十二種發憤？一、偽斗，二、偽稱，三、偽函，四、邪業方便，五、拒鬪，六、輕調，七、違反，八、諍訟，九、罵詈，十、忿怒，十一、訶責，十二、迫脅，十三、捶打，十四、殺害，十五、繫縛，十六、禁閉，十七、割截，十八、驅擯，十九、諂曲，二十、矯誑，二十一、陷逗，二十二、妄語。
items.en: What are the twenty-two occasions for anger? First, a false measuring-basket. Second, a false scale. Third, a forged document. Fourth, devious means towards wrongdoing. Fifth, resistance and conflict. Sixth, being mocked. Seventh, being defied. Eighth, litigation and dispute. Ninth, being cursed and reviled. Tenth, another's fury. Eleventh, being reproached. Twelfth, being threatened. Thirteenth, being beaten. Fourteenth, being killed. Fifteenth, being bound. Sixteenth, being imprisoned. Seventeenth, being mutilated. Eighteenth, being expelled. Nineteenth, flattery and duplicity. Twentieth, deceit and pretence. Twenty-first, being lured into a trap. Twenty-second, being lied to.

items.zh: 云何六十二種有情之類？

一、那洛迦，二、傍生，三、鬼，四、天，五、人，六、剎帝利，七、婆羅門，八、吠舍，九、戍陀羅，十、女，十一、男，十二、非男非女，十三、劣，十四、中，十五、妙，十六、在家，十七、出家，十八、苦行，十九、非苦行，二十、律儀，二十一、不律儀，二十二、非律儀非不律儀，二十三、離欲，二十四、未離欲，二十五、邪性聚定，二十六、正性聚定，二十七、不定聚定，二十八、苾芻，二十九、苾芻尼，三十、正學，三十一、勤策男，三十二、勤策女，三十三、近事男，三十四、近事女，
items.en: 1. Hell-beings; 2. animals; 3. hungry ghosts; 4. gods; 5. humans; 6. kṣatriyas; 7. brāhmaṇas; 8. vaiśyas; 9. śūdras; 10. females; 11. males; 12. those neither male nor female; 13. the inferior; 14. the middling; 15. the excellent; 16. householders; 17. renunciants; 18. those who practice austerities; 19. those who do not; 20. the disciplined; 21. the undisciplined; 22. those neither disciplined nor undisciplined; 23. those free of desire; 24. those not yet free of desire; 25. those fixed in the wrong group; 26. those fixed in the right group; 27. those in the undetermined group; 28. monks; 29. nuns; 30. female probationers; 31. male novices; 32. female novices; 33. laymen; 34. laywomen.

items.zh: 三十五、習斷者，三十六、習誦者，三十七、淨施人，三十八、宿長，三十九、中年，四十、少年，四十一、軌範師，四十二、親教師，四十三、共住弟子及近住弟子，四十四、賓客，四十五、營僧事者，四十六、貪利養恭敬者，四十七、厭捨者，四十八、多聞者，四十九、大福智者，五十、法隨法行者，五十一、持經者，五十二、持律者，五十三、持論者，
items.en: 35. Those who practice cutting off affliction; 36. those who practice recitation; 37. those who make pure donation; 38. elders; 39. those of middle age; 40. the young; 41. preceptor-instructors; 42. ordaining masters; 43. resident and neighbouring disciples; 44. guests; 45. those who manage the community's affairs; 46. those attached to gain and honour; 47. those who have renounced such things; 48. the learned; 49. those of great merit and wisdom; 50. those who practice in accordance with the Dharma; 51. keepers of the sūtras; 52. keepers of the vinaya; 53. keepers of the treatises.

items.zh: 五十四、異生，五十五、見諦，五十六、有學，五十七、無學，五十八、聲聞，五十九、獨覺，六十、菩薩，六十一、如來，六十二、轉輪王。
items.en: 54. Ordinary worldlings; 55. those who have seen the truth; 56. those still in training; 57. those beyond training; 58. śrāvakas; 59. pratyekabuddhas; 60. bodhisattvas; 61. tathāgatas; 62. wheel-turning kings.

items.zh: 此轉輪王復有四種。或王一洲，或二三四。王一洲者，有鐵輪應；王二洲者，有銅輪應；王三洲者，有銀輪應；王四洲者，有金輪應。
items.en: This wheel-turning king is, moreover, of four kinds: ruling one continent, or two, three, or four. One who rules a single continent has the iron wheel appear in response; one who rules two continents has the bronze wheel; one who rules three continents has the silver wheel; one who rules all four continents has the golden wheel.

items.zh: 云何八位？謂處胎位、出生位、嬰孩位、童子位、少年位、中年位、老年位、耄熟位。處胎位者，謂羯羅藍等。出生位者，謂從此後乃至耄熟。嬰孩位者，謂乃至未能遊行嬉戲。
items.en: What are the eight stages? The stage in the womb, the stage of birth, the stage of infancy, the stage of childhood, the stage of youth, the stage of middle age, the stage of old age, and the stage of advanced old age. The stage in the womb is the kalala and the stages that follow it. The stage of birth extends from this point onward, up to advanced old age. The stage of infancy lasts until one is able to walk about and play.

items.zh: 童子位者，謂能為彼事。少年位者，謂能受用欲塵，乃至三十。中年位者，謂從此位乃至五十。老年位者，謂從此位乃至七十。從此以上，名耄熟位。
items.en: The stage of childhood is when one becomes able to do so. The stage of youth is when one is able to enjoy the objects of desire, up to the age of thirty. The stage of middle age extends from there up to fifty. The stage of old age extends from there up to seventy. Beyond this is called the stage of advanced old age.

items.title: Four Ways of Entering the Womb — With or Without Awareness

items.zh: 云何四種入胎？一、正知而入，不正知住出；二、正知入住，不正知而出；三、俱能正知；四、俱不正知。
items.en: What are the four ways of entering the womb? First, entering with clear awareness, but dwelling and emerging without it. Second, entering and dwelling with clear awareness, but emerging without it. Third, being clearly aware throughout all three — entering, dwelling, and emerging. Fourth, being aware in none of the three.

items.zh: 初謂輪王，二謂獨覺，三謂菩薩，四謂所餘有情。

items.title: Six Ways to Make a Living, Six Kinds of Protection

items.zh: 云何六種活命？一、營農，二、商賈，三、牧牛，四、事王，五、習學書算計數及印，六、習學所餘工巧業處。
items.en: What are the six ways of making a living? First, farming. Second, trade. Third, herding cattle. Fourth, serving the king. Fifth, the study of writing, arithmetic, and accounting. Sixth, the study of other skilled crafts.

items.zh: 云何六種守護？謂象軍、馬軍、車軍、步軍、藏力、友力。
items.en: What are the six kinds of protection? The elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, the infantry, the power of the storehouse, and the power of friends.

blocks.text: More short lists describing ordinary life in the world: things we must attend to again and again, kinds of speech, occasions for anger, sixty-two kinds of beings, wheel-turning kings, the stages of a life, ways of entering the womb, livelihoods, and protections. Read them as a portrait of the human condition drawn up by meditators. The commentary picks out the items our teachers dwell on.

Untranslated: 0288c26, the question "What are the sixty-two kinds of beings?"; and 0289a29–b01, which identifies the four ways of entering the womb with the wheel-turning king, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva, and all other beings.

subs.head: Things to attend to again and again

blocks.text: The "eight recurring necessities" (數數事) include washing, eating, sleeping, and the like. Venerable Miào Jìng notes that 數 is read *shuò*, "again and again". Master Cháng Bǎi adds that none of the eight is a fault in itself; the treatise simply shows how much of life is maintenance.

Speech in accord with the Dharma, not in accord with it, and other speech. Master Cháng Bǎi: the same topic can fall into any of the three depending on the mind behind it. Talk about family or food spoken with craving or resentment is not in accord with the Dharma; spoken with no particular intention, it is "other speech"; only speech that leads towards the good is in accord with the Dharma.

The list begins with cheating: a false measuring-basket, a false scale, a forged document. Venerable Miào Jìng explains the basket: smaller when selling, larger when buying. Master Cháng Bǎi reads the whole list as moving from material deception, through open conflict and physical harm, to subtler dishonesty. It is a list of the things people do that provoke anger in others, useful for examining one's own conduct.

The longest list of the fascicle classifies beings every possible way: by realm, by class and occupation, by lay or ordained life, by stage of practice, by gender, and so on, ending with noble beings and Buddhas. Its purpose is not to rank but to show the variety of conditions karma produces.

A **wheel-turning king** (轉輪王, *cakravartin*) rules by the power of a wheel that "appears in response" to his merit: iron for one continent, bronze for two, silver for three, gold for all four. Master Cháng Bǎi adds a gloss on how they rule: the golden-wheel king need do nothing and neighbouring realms submit of themselves; the silver must travel and be seen; the bronze must persuade; the iron must show force. The less virtue, the more coercion.

In the womb; birth; childhood; youth; adulthood; middle age; old age; extreme old age. Venerable Miào Jìng notes that "the stage of birth" in this list covers everything "from coming out of the mother's womb all the way to advanced old age", while in Day 8's account birth meant only the moment of emerging.

subs.head: Four ways of entering the womb

blocks.text: Beings differ in how much awareness they keep: some enter aware but dwell and emerge unaware; some enter and dwell aware but emerge unaware; some are aware throughout; most are aware in none. The untranslated line assigns these to the wheel-turning king, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva in his last life, and all other beings, which Master Cháng Bǎi's lecture also gives.

Venerable Miào Jìng uses this to correct a common Chinese saying, "even a stream-enterer is confused between lives" (須陀洹尚有隔陰之迷). Those who have actually attained the noble path, he says, are not confused; texts that speak of stream-enterers entering unaware mean those who will attain the fruit later in that life.

The livelihoods are farming, trade, herding, service to a king, writing and calculation, and crafts. The protections are elephants, cavalry, chariots, infantry, "the power of the storehouse", and "the power of friends". Both teachers read "the storehouse" (藏力) as the ālayavijñāna itself, which protects a being simply by sustaining its body; Venerable Miào Jìng adds that 藏 also suggests self-love, the guarding of self and "mine". Even in a list about armies, the treatise slips in the eighth consciousness.

quiz.q: The treatise speaks of "the eight recurring necessities — the things worldly beings must attend to again and again (數數)." According to Venerable Miào Jìng, how should 數 be read and understood here?
options: read shù, meaning a number
read shǔ, meaning to count
read shuò, meaning again and again, repeatedly
read cù, meaning fine or dense
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "This 數 should not be read *shù*; it should be read *shuò* — 'again and again,' things that must be done all the time." The translation's "recurring necessities" and "again and again" carry the same sense. Master Cháng Bǎi notes that none of the eight is itself a fault; they simply describe what a body in the world requires. Venerable Miào Jìng adds that gods of the form realm do not sleep, while even an arhat with supernormal powers still needs sleep physically.

quiz.q: The treatise distinguishes three kinds of speech: in accord with the Dharma, not in accord with it, and other speech. Taking the two teachers together, which is correct?
options: the classification depends on the mind behind the speech: the same topic can fall into any of the three; speech in and not in accord with the Dharma both come from a determinate mind, while other speech comes from an indeterminate mind
it depends on the topic: talk of Dharma is in accord, talk of food is not
only monastics' speech can be in accord with the Dharma
"other speech" is just another name for speech not in accord with the Dharma
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the very same topic — food, family, current events — can fall into any of the three depending on the mind behind it: spoken with craving or resentment, it is not in accord with the Dharma; with neither wholesome nor unwholesome intent, it is other speech; only speech that leads towards renunciation and freedom from affliction is in accord. Venerable Miào Jìng: speech from an indeterminate mind is "other speech," "which shows that speech in accord with the Dharma and speech not in accord are both from a determinate mind." B looks only at the text's example, "speech about food, drink, and the like," and ignores "spoken with a defiled mind."

quiz.q: What are the first three of the twenty-two occasions for anger?
options: being cursed, another's fury, being reproached
a false measuring-basket, a false scale, a forged document
being killed, bound, imprisoned
flattery, deceit, being lied to
quiz.why: "First, a false measuring-basket. Second, a false scale. Third, a forged document." Master Cháng Bǎi reads the whole list as moving from material deception (rigged measures, forged documents), through open conflict, to physical harm, and finally to subtler dishonesty. A gives items nine to eleven, C fourteen to sixteen, and D nineteen, twenty, and twenty-two.

quiz.q: The treatise says each of the four kinds of wheel-turning king has a wheel appear in response. Which pairing is correct?
options: one continent, iron wheel; two, bronze; three, silver; four, golden
one continent, golden wheel; four, iron
one continent, silver wheel; two, golden
all four have the golden wheel
quiz.why: "One who rules a single continent has the iron wheel appear in response; one who rules two continents has the bronze wheel; one who rules three continents has the silver wheel; one who rules all four continents has the golden wheel." Venerable Miào Jìng: "appear in response" means the wheel appears of itself, not made by anyone; the two continents are the eastern and southern ones, and the three add the western. Minor kings ruling only part of one continent are called "scattered-millet kings."

quiz.q: How long does "the stage of birth," among the eight stages, last according to the treatise?
options: from emerging from the womb onward, all the way to advanced old age
only the moment of emerging from the birth canal
the first month after birth
until one can walk about and play
quiz.why: "The stage of birth extends from this point onward, up to advanced old age." Venerable Miào Jìng stresses this: "From coming out of the mother's womb all the way to advanced old age — all of it is called the stage of birth." B describes §17's "the moment it emerges from the birth canal is called the stage of actual birth," the closest trap; D is the boundary of infancy. He glosses 熟 in 耄熟 as "extreme" — very advanced in age.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT among the four ways of entering the womb listed in the treatise?
options: entering with clear awareness, but dwelling and emerging without it
being clearly aware throughout all three
being aware in none of the three
entering without awareness, but dwelling and emerging with it
quiz.why: The four are: entering with awareness but dwelling and emerging without it; entering and dwelling with awareness but emerging without it; aware throughout all three; and aware in none. Awareness is kept progressively — from entering, to dwelling, to emerging — so there is no case of entering unaware yet dwelling and emerging aware. Master Cháng Bǎi reads the sequence as measuring how fully a mind has mastered the process of rebirth.

quiz.q: Among the six kinds of protection is "the power of the storehouse" (藏力). How do both teachers explain it?
options: the financial strength of the treasury
the ālayavijñāna — by continuing to sustain the body, it gives the most basic protection (Venerable Miào Jìng adds that 藏 is self-love: guarding self and what is "mine")
a hidden army
the scriptures stored in a monastery
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the first four (elephant, cavalry, chariot, infantry) are an ordinary kingdom's military defenses; "the power of the storehouse" is the ālayavijñāna itself, which protects a being simply by continuing to sustain the body; "the power of friends" is the goodwill of family, companions, and teachers. Venerable Miào Jìng: "What is this 藏? It is the ālayavijñāna; this 藏 is self-love … clinging to a self and to what is mine — that is 'storing and guarding.'" A is the reading one would guess from the characters, which neither teacher adopts. Note that for "the matter of one's stored wealth" in §48, he takes 藏 as stored wealth.
